title: Judges 9:7–21
context: From Mount Gerizim, Jotham tells a fable: the trees seek a king, and the olive, fig, and vine each decline, unwilling to give up their useful fruit. Only the bramble accepts, offering shade it cannot give and threatening fire if refused. Jotham then applies the story, asking whether Shechem has acted in good faith toward Gideon’s house. If not, he says, let fire come from Abimelech and Shechem to consume each other. He then flees to Beer.

verses.text: When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood on the top of Mount Gerizim and lifted up his voice, cried out, and said to them, “Listen to me, you men of Shechem, that God may listen to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham stands on Mount Gerizim and calls the men of Shechem to listen so that God may listen to them. Arminian readers note the setting, the mountain of blessing in Deuteronomy 11:29, used here to deliver a warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jotham speaking as a lone, prophet-like witness who appeals to God as judge. Shared ground: his words frame the fable as a test of Shechem’s faithfulness, with God’s hearing tied to whether they have acted justly.

verses.text: The trees set out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
verses.arminianNotes: The trees set out to anoint a king and turn first to the olive tree. Arminian readers note that the fable’s opening mirrors Shechem’s choice, as a community decides for itself to seek a ruler over it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that anointing language recalls how kings were later set apart in Israel. Both traditions read the fable as political wisdom about leadership rather than as a direct statement about kingship in principle, and neither forces a theological fork here.

verses.text: “But the olive tree said to them, ‘Should I stop producing my oil, with which they honor God and man by me, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
verses.arminianNotes: The olive tree refuses to give up its oil, which honors God and man, to wave over the trees. Arminian readers see the point that worthy people often decline power because they are already fruitful in their proper work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that oil was used in worship and anointing, so the olive’s usefulness is tied to honoring God. Shared ground: the fable treats ruling as “waving over” the trees, a picture that questions the value of grasping for power.

verses.text: “The trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’
verses.arminianNotes: The trees next ask the fig tree to reign. Arminian readers note the repeated pattern of the fable, which builds by asking one productive tree after another, each of which will offer a reason to decline the throne.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as a storyteller’s device that sharpens the contrast with the bramble. Both traditions read the fig tree’s place in the sequence as part of a single argument about who seeks power and who does not.

verses.text: “But the fig tree said to them, ‘Should I leave my sweetness, and my good fruit, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
verses.arminianNotes: The fig tree will not leave its sweetness and good fruit. Arminian readers see a picture of contentment with one’s calling, in contrast to Abimelech, who was willing to kill his brothers to seize what he was not given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fig’s sweetness stands for real goodness that would be lost in exchange for empty status. Shared ground: the fable honors useful, humble service above the pursuit of rule over others.

verses.text: “The trees said to the vine, ‘Come and reign over us.’
verses.arminianNotes: The trees turn to the vine. Arminian readers note that the request is now almost desperate, as the trees keep looking for someone willing to accept the crown they are so eager to bestow on another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the fable’s three refusals leave readers expecting the worst choice to come last. Both traditions read the vine’s turn as the final step before the bramble, building tension toward Jotham’s main point.

verses.text: “The vine said to them, ‘Should I leave my new wine, which cheers God and man, and go to wave back and forth over the trees?’
verses.arminianNotes: The vine refuses to give up its new wine, which cheers God and man. Arminian readers note the language of wine used in offerings (compare Numbers 15:7–10), and see the vine’s joy as a gift it will not trade away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the refusals together as showing that fruitful things serve God and people where they are. Shared ground: the olive, fig, and vine each prefer faithful usefulness to ruling, and the fable invites the hearers to notice who remains.

verses.text: “Then all the trees said to the bramble, ‘Come and reign over us.’
verses.arminianNotes: At last all the trees ask the bramble to reign. Arminian readers see a pointed image: when good candidates decline, a community may settle for the least fit leader, one who has nothing to lose by taking power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the bramble bears no fruit and offers little shade, a fitting picture of Abimelech. Both traditions read the trees’ unanimous choice as Shechem’s folly in making a worthless and dangerous man their king.

verses.text: “The bramble said to the trees, ‘If in truth you anoint me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon.’
verses.arminianNotes: The bramble invites the trees to take refuge in its shade or else be consumed by fire. Arminian readers note the absurd offer of shelter from a thorn bush, joined to a threat that reveals the bramble’s true nature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fire that could devour even the cedars of Lebanon as a warning that tyranny destroys the great as well as the small. Shared ground: the fable’s conclusion is a prophecy of destruction that the rest of the chapter fulfills.

verses.text: “Now therefore, if you have dealt truly and righteously, in that you have made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, and have done to him according to the deserving of his hands
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham turns to the application: have they acted truly and righteously in making Abimelech king? Arminian readers stress that he holds the men of Shechem accountable for a choice they freely made and could have refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the conditional form and its focus on how Shechem treated Gideon’s house. Both traditions read the question as an appeal to justice, with the long sentence running on into a parenthesis in the verses that follow.

verses.text: (for my father fought for you, risked his life, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian;
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham reminds them that Gideon fought, risked his life, and delivered them from Midian. Arminian readers see an appeal to gratitude, since Shechem benefited from his deliverance and should not have repaid him with violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the deliverance from Midian was the LORD’s work through Gideon (7:2, 7), so turning on his house disregards that grace. Shared ground: ingratitude toward a deliverer is part of Shechem’s guilt.

verses.text: and you have risen up against my father’s house today and have slain his sons, seventy persons, on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother);
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham names the crime: the men of Shechem have killed seventy sons on one stone and crowned Abimelech, the son of a female servant, because he is their brother. Arminian readers note that he lays the guilt on Shechem as well as on Abimelech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the indictment as joining kinship politics and bloodshed into a single charge. Both traditions note that Jotham presents Shechem as an active partner in the massacre, not a bystander to it.

verses.text: if you then have dealt truly and righteously with Jerubbaal and with his house today, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you;
verses.arminianNotes: If they have acted rightly, Jotham says, let them rejoice in Abimelech and he in them. Arminian readers see heavy irony, since the conditions plainly have not been met and the blessing therefore cannot apply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the rhetorical structure that leaves the hearers to supply the obvious answer. Shared ground: the verse sets up the curse in the next verse by offering a blessing that Shechem has already forfeited by its conduct.

verses.text: but if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo and devour Abimelech.”
verses.arminianNotes: If not, let fire come from Abimelech and Shechem to devour each other. Arminian readers see a curse that names mutual destruction as the natural fruit of a partnership built on violence and betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the curse will be fulfilled in detail, including fire at the tower of Shechem (9:49), and that the narrator links it to God’s repayment (9:57). Both traditions read the curse as an appeal to God’s justice.

verses.text: Jotham ran away and fled, and went to Beer and lived there, for fear of Abimelech his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham flees to Beer and lives there for fear of Abimelech. WEB notes that Beer means “well,” a village named for its well; its location is uncertain. Arminian readers see a lone witness who speaks the truth and then escapes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jotham leaves the matter in God’s hands rather than taking revenge himself. Shared ground: the youngest son, the only survivor, delivers his word and departs, and the narrative now waits to see how it will be fulfilled.
